subject: Biology
title: Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium
description: A micro-lesson that makes Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium usable.

hook.text: In a perfect, unchanging world, allele frequencies would stay the same forever. They never do.

buildup.text: The Hardy-Weinberg principle predicts allele frequencies when no evolution is occurring.

discovery.text: It requires no selection, no mutation, no migration, random mating, and infinite population size.

twist.text: No real population meets all five conditions—so Hardy-Weinberg is a null model, not reality.

climax.text: Scientists use it to detect evolution. If frequencies deviate from the prediction, something is changing.

punchline.text: The model of no evolution helps us measure real evolution.

quiz.question: What does the Hardy-Weinberg model assume?
options: No selection, mutation, migration, random mating, and large population

details.summary: The Hardy-Weinberg principle states that allele frequencies in a population remain constant across generations if no evolution occurs. Its five assumptions, no selection, no mutation, no migration, no drift, and random mating, are never fully met, making it a null model against which real evoluti...
details.whyItMatters: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is the baseline for detecting evolution. When real populations deviate from its predictions, scientists can pinpoint which evolutionary force is acting, making it an essential diagnostic tool in population genetics.
takeaways: The equation p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1 predicts genotype frequencies from allele frequencies
Any deviation from Hardy-Weinberg indicates evolutionary forces are acting
The principle requires five conditions that are never perfectly met in nature

faq.question: Why is Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium useful if it never exists in nature?
faq.answer: It serves as a null hypothesis. By comparing observed genotype frequencies to Hardy-Weinberg predictions, scientists detect when evolution is occurring and which assumptions are violated. It is like a control experiment for detecting evolutionary forces.

faq.question: What are the five conditions required for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
faq.answer: No natural selection, no mutation, no gene flow or migration, no genetic drift meaning an infinitely large population, and random mating. Violating any condition causes allele frequencies to change, which is evolution by definition.
